emails.title: Welcome from Karlin
emails.job: Who Karlin is and why he started EKUZO. Bridges back to the ad they saw.

copy.subject: Their spot for season one is saved. Here's what's next.
copy.preview: Structure beats screen time limits. A note from our founder on what that looks like.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, I'm Karlin.

blocks.text: Thanks for joining the Season 01 waitlist. If our ad about screen time hit a little close to home, you're not alone. It's the reason I started EKUZO.
Like most kids, I cared most about video games and screens. And like most parents, mine thought they were the root of all my problems.
For the most part, they were right. Right up until I got a video game scholarship that paid for college.
Most families are constantly at war with screen time, stuck between taking it away and limiting it. I think there's a third option: give them a team and the tools to get better.
That's the structure of what we're building. A league where kids practice with legit coaches, rep a jersey with their gamer tag, and get better with their team every week.
This is less about screen time and more about your kid doing something they love, in a way that makes you proud.
Over the next few weeks, I'll show you exactly how it works: what practice looks like, what they learn, and what you'll see at home.
Glad you're here.

copy.ps: If you made it this far, you're the kind of parent we're building this for. Hit reply and tell me about your kid. I read every one.

emails.title: What we do
emails.job: The whole idea in one easy read: build the team, meet the coach, practice.

copy.subject: Here's how it actually works
copy.preview: A team, a coach, and a night on the calendar. The short version.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, here's the short version.

blocks.text: A couple of days ago I told you why I started EKUZO. Today I want to show you what it actually is. It comes down to three things.

blocks.head: Build the team
blocks.text: Your kid joins a small team of kids around their age and level. Same teammates every week, a jersey with their gamer tag on it, and a team that has their back.

blocks.head: Meet the coach
blocks.text: Every practice is run by a coach who has played at a high level and chose to coach kids. They know the game. They also know the game is the easy part.

blocks.head: Practice
blocks.text: One night a week, on the calendar, with their team and their coach. It has a plan, and it quickly becomes the night they look forward to.

blocks.head: If they love gaming, they're ready.
blocks.text: Most kids start with a game they've never played, so everyone learns it together, with a coach, a team and a plan.
Over the next few emails I'll take these one at a time, starting with the team: who's on it, how it comes together, and why it matters more than the game.

copy.ps: What made you sign up? Something your kid said, or something you've been thinking about for a while? Hit reply. I read every one.

emails.title: Screen time, reconsidered
emails.job: Challenge the hours question. Same screen, very different nights. From our blog: what your kid's gaming is telling you.

copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, let's talk about screen time.
copy.preview: Not how many hours. What the game is doing for them.
copy.subject: The screen time question I'd ask instead
copy.ps: What's one thing your kid says about gaming that you've never quite known how to answer? Hit reply. I read every one.

blocks.text: Almost every parent I talk to asks some version of the same question: how much is too much?

It's a fair question. But two kids can play the exact same hours and be having completely different nights. One is on a headset with the same four friends, talking, laughing, figuring something out together. The other is alone in a lobby full of strangers, getting louder with every loss.
From the hallway, those look the same. They aren't.
So before counting hours, try reading the game. A few clues our team has written about:

blocks.head: Big reactions
blocks.text: When a loss turns into a meltdown, the size of the reaction usually tells you the size of what's riding on it. Somewhere in that game, they've found something they're good at.

blocks.head: Who they play with
blocks.text: The same people over time, talking and on a team, is connection. Strangers in a different lobby every night is something else. The screen looks the same either way.

blocks.head: What they don't say
blocks.text: About 85% of teens play video games, but only about 4 in 10 call themselves gamers. A lot of kids care more than they'll admit.
None of this means hours don't matter. It means the hours are usually downstream of something else, and that's the part worth getting curious about.

blocks.head: Read: What your kid's gaming is telling you

emails.title: Their team
emails.job: Online friends, real team. The difference is the same people every week. From our blog: when your son's only friends are online.

copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, let's talk about their team.
copy.preview: Connection and isolation look the same from the hallway.
copy.subject: Why the same four friends matter more than the game
copy.ps: Does your kid play with the same friends most nights, or mostly with strangers? Hit reply. I'm curious.

blocks.text: Teens spend about 71% less time with friends in person than they did in the early 2000s. It's easy to blame the screen.

But when researchers read what kids actually say to each other mid-game, the social stuff (“what's up,” “you good?”) outnumbered the strategy talk more than three to one. For a lot of kids, a headset full of teammates is how friendships get built.
The difference is whether it's the same people every week.

blocks.head: Same kids, every week
blocks.text: Your kid joins a small team of kids around their age and level. They learn each other's voices, habits and jokes. By week three, they're not strangers anymore.

blocks.head: Their name on a jersey
blocks.text: It sounds small. Watch your kid's face when theirs shows up with their gamer tag on the back.

blocks.head: A team that has their back
blocks.text: Wins are fun. The real moment is a rough night, when a teammate says “we got the next one” and means it.

blocks.head: Read: When your son's only friends are online

emails.title: Practice night
emails.job: One practice night, start to finish, told for fun: their friends, a plan, real play, the review. Facts to confirm: length, night, team size, online or in person.

copy.subject: What a practice night actually looks like
copy.preview: Headsets on, friends in the call, and a plan for the night.
copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, here's a practice night.

blocks.text: Last time I said I'd show you how this works. Here's one practice night, start to finish.

blocks.title: Logging in
blocks.text: Headset on. Their teammates are already in the call, talking about whatever happened at school today. Same kids every week, around the same age.

blocks.title: The plan
blocks.text: The coach opens with one thing the team is working on tonight. Something specific, like calling out what they see before it's too late.

blocks.title: Play
blocks.text: They play together while the coach listens in. This is the part you'll hear through the door: callouts, groans, and a lot of laughing.

blocks.title: The review
blocks.text: They watch back a moment from tonight, a fight they lost or a play that worked, and figure out why together. Nobody gets blamed. Everyone leaves with one thing to try next week.

blocks.title: GG
blocks.text: Everyone says good game. They log off already talking about next week.
What I hope you notice first isn't the gaming. It's that your kid has somewhere to be, people counting on them, and something to tell you about at dinner.

copy.ps: Which night is the hardest one in your house when it comes to gaming? Hit reply and tell me. It'll help us pick Season 01 practice nights.

emails.title: Worlds is in the US
emails.job: Real time. The League of Legends World Championship is in the US this year (Swiss stage in Allen, TX Oct 23-31, final Nov 14 in Brooklyn). Invite parents to watch 20 minutes with their kid. Send as a one-off campaign, not in the flow.

copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, the world championship is here.
copy.preview: Free to watch, and a great way to see gaming the way your kid does.
copy.subject: The World Series of esports is in Texas this month
copy.ps: If you watch, hit reply and tell me what your kid said. I'd love to know what they noticed.

blocks.text: Every fall, the best teams on the planet meet at the League of Legends World Championship. Think of it as the World Series of esports.
This year it's in the US. The main stage runs in Allen, Texas, and the final is Saturday, November 14 at Barclays Center in Brooklyn. Big arena, big crowd, the whole thing.
Here's my ask: watch twenty minutes of it with your kid.

Not to learn the game. Most kids who join us have never played it. Watch the crowd, the players' faces, and the way five teammates talk each other through the hard moments. Then ask your kid what they'd want to be great at.

blocks.head: How to watch
blocks.text: Free on YouTube, Twitch and lolesports.com. Swiss stage: Oct 23 to 31. Quarterfinals: Nov 3 to 6. Semifinals: Nov 7 and 8. Final: Saturday, Nov 14 at 2pm Eastern.
Three North American teams made it: Team Liquid, LYON and Cloud9. If you need someone to root for, pick one together.

emails.title: Meet the coach
emails.job: The people who run practice, told through one coach. Coach Muhammad, who spent the summer listening to parents. From our blog: should you ban Fortnite.

copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, meet Coach Muhammad.
copy.preview: He spent his summer listening to parents. Here's what he heard.
copy.subject: Meet one of the people who'd coach your kid
copy.ps: If you could ask a coach one question before your kid's first practice, what would it be? Hit reply.

blocks.text: Every EKUZO practice is run by a coach. I want you to meet one of them.

Muhammad is a senior at Texas A&M and coaches League of Legends for us. This summer, part of his job was listening. He sat down with parents and wrote down what actually happens in their houses around gaming.
One of them was Casey, a mom of two who banned Fortnite. The ban worked. Then a new problem showed up, because the game had been quietly doing a job in her family.
What she did next is the useful part. She started judging games one at a time, by the kid each one handed back to her.
That's the kind of coach I want with your kid. Someone who listens first, to the kids and to you.

emails.title: A family's story
emails.job: What parents see at home, through one family. Ryan (K1ng) and his mom, in her words. From our blog. One family's experience, not a promise.

copy.headline: Hi {first_name}, meet Ryan and his mom.
copy.preview: One mom on what changed when her son found his team.
copy.subject: “We can hear him when he plays, and it's a wonderful thing”
copy.ps: What would make you proud of your kid a year from now? Hit reply. I read every one.

blocks.text: Ryan was 12 when his school sent home an email about a new esports team. He'd never heard of esports. He'd never played League of Legends. He signed up anyway.
He was one of the youngest players on the team. Within his first year, his teammates were choosing him to lead in tournaments. His in-game name is K1ngofbattle. Everyone calls him K1ng.
“We can hear him when he plays, and it's a wonderful thing.”
That's his mom. She says he hypes up his team, praises his teammates, and that it's fun for parents to watch because the kids have so much fun together.
Ryan's story is one family's experience, not a promise. But it's the reason I do this: a kid who found his people, and parents who got to be proud of what they heard through the door.
